title: In defence of nostalgia
text: Nostalgia began its career as a disease. In 1688 a Swiss physician coined the word to describe mercenaries whose longing for home was thought to {{1}} (THREAT) their very lives; the prescribed cures, which ranged from leeches to threats of live burial, now read as genuinely {{2}} (APPAL). Modern psychology has rehabilitated the feeling altogether. Far from being a sickness, a wistful turn through personal memory now appears remarkably {{3}} (HEALTH): experiments show that nostalgic reflection makes people feel more {{4}} (CONNECT) to others, raises self-esteem, increases optimism about the future and even renders people slightly more {{5}} (GENEROSITY) to strangers. The trigger is usually {{6}} (SENSE) — a song, a smell of school corridors, the taste of a discontinued sweet — and the effect arrives within minutes. Contrary to stereotype, it is not pensioners who indulge most: adolescents report the strongest nostalgia of all, perhaps because the {{7}} (IDENTIFY) of the self is still under construction and needs its materials. Researchers now describe the emotion as less a longing for what is gone than a tool for the present — a naturally occurring {{8}} (RESTORE) that the mind dispenses exactly when belonging and courage run low.

gaps.explanation: 'thought to threaten their lives' — verb from threat.
'read as genuinely appalling' — the cures cause horror (British spelling).
'feel more connected to others' — passive participle from connect.
'slightly more generous to strangers' — the adjective of this family is generous.

gaps.hint: adjective: to do with the senses
gaps.explanation: 'The trigger is usually sensory' — adjective from sense.
'the identity of the self' — the noun of this family is identity.
'a naturally occurring restorative' — adjective from restore.
